topic: Finger sprains and jams in ball sports

slides.headline: Jammed a finger catching the ball?
slides.sub: Why tugging it straight isn't the move, and what helps instead.

slides.title: Skip the tug-it-back trick
slides.body: Pulling on a jammed finger can stress the same ligaments that just got sprained. Instead, step off the court, cool it with a wrapped cold pack and keep your hand raised for a while.

slides.title: Buddy taping: the useful bit
slides.body: Taping the sore finger to its neighbour gives support while still letting it bend. Put a little padding between the fingers, keep the tape snug rather than tight, and redo it if the skin gets irritated.

slides.title: Keep the other joints moving
slides.body: Gently bending the knuckles you can move, plus making a loose fist a few times an hour, usually stops the whole hand stiffening up. Some puffiness around a finger joint can linger for weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A fingertip that won't straighten on its own, a joint that looks bent or out of place, numbness, big swelling or trouble gripping a cup are worth an assessment soon, as some need early splinting.

slides.title: Easing back into the game
slides.body: Most people return with tape on first. Test the finger with gripping, pinching and easy catching drills before a full game. Cricket, netball and beach volleyball season all put fingers in the firing line.

caption:
Jammed a finger catching the ball this summer? Put down the urge to yank it straight.

Finger sprains are common in cricket, netball, basketball and beach volleyball. Pulling on the joint can stress the ligaments that were just injured, so cool it, raise it and keep the other knuckles moving gently.

Buddy taping to the next finger gives support while still letting it bend. Most jammed fingers settle with time, though a puffy joint can hang around for a few weeks.

A fingertip that won't straighten, a joint that looks out of place, numbness or big swelling are worth getting checked soon, as some finger injuries do better with early splinting.
